unit.title: History and lore
unit.summary: Legends, rivalries, safety milestones and why certain places matter.

lessons.title: The champions and their counts
lessons.objective: Place Fangio, Schumacher, Hamilton, Verstappen and the 2025 champion.

payload.prompt: Juan Manuel Fangio was world champion in the 1950s. How many titles did he win?

options.text: 2 titles
options.explanation: Too few. Fangio was one of the sport's first superstars.

options.text: 5 titles
options.explanation: Right. Five titles between 1951 and 1957, a record that stood until Schumacher passed it in 2003.

options.text: 7 titles
options.explanation: Seven is the record shared by Hamilton and Schumacher. Fangio won five.

options.text: 3 titles
options.explanation: Three would be more like Senna or Stewart. Fangio won more.

explanation.correct: Fangio won five world titles, in 1951 and from 1954 to 1957, with four different teams. His record stood until Michael Schumacher passed it in 2003.
explanation.incorrect: Fangio won five drivers' titles in the 1950s. That was the record until Schumacher won his sixth in 2003.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fangio won five titles, in the 1950s.

payload.prompt: Michael Schumacher's Ferrari dominated in the 2000s. How many constructors' titles did Ferrari win in that era?

options.text: 1 title
options.explanation: Ferrari did better than that in the Schumacher years.

options.text: 3 titles
options.explanation: Close, but Ferrari's dominance was deeper.

options.text: 6 titles between 1999 and 2004
options.explanation: Right. Six team championships in six years; Schumacher won the drivers' title five times in that run.

options.text: 2 titles
options.explanation: Ferrari won more than that during Schumacher's era.

explanation.correct: Right. Ferrari won six consecutive constructors' championships from 1999 to 2004. The drivers' title was held by Schumacher five times in that span.
explanation.incorrect: Ferrari's six-year run with Schumacher (1999–2004) remains one of the most dominant spells in the sport. Both the drivers' and constructors' titles were nearly always red.
explanation.sayThisLine: Schumacher and Ferrari owned the 2000s with six team titles in a row.

payload.prompt: Match each champion to their title story.

pairs.definition: Seven titles: one with McLaren, six with Mercedes.
Four in a row, from 2021 to 2024, with Red Bull.
Five titles in the 1950s, the first great record.
Seven titles: two with Benetton, five with Ferrari.

explanation.summary: Seven is the record: Schumacher got there first, Hamilton matched him. Verstappen has four, Fangio set the first big mark with five.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hamilton and Schumacher share the record on seven.

payload.prompt: Match each team to its constructors' titles.

pairs.definition: 16 constructors' titles, the most of any team.
9 constructors' titles, mostly in the 1980s and 1990s.

distractorDefinitions: Three titles and a long wait since.

explanation.summary: Ferrari is the record holder. Williams was the dominant force in the 1980s and 1990s, and Mercedes ran a modern streak of eight straight.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari has the record, Mercedes the longest streak.

payload.prompt: Who won the 2025 drivers' championship?

options.text: Lando Norris, for McLaren.
options.explanation: Right. Norris won the title in a close three-way fight, and McLaren also took the constructors' title.

options.text: Max Verstappen, for Red Bull.
options.explanation: Verstappen won the four titles before it and finished close in 2025, but he did not win it.

options.text: Charles Leclerc, for Ferrari.
options.explanation: Leclerc has not won a title yet.

options.text: George Russell, for Mercedes.
options.explanation: Russell was in the fight at times, but he did not win the title.

explanation.correct: Lando Norris won the 2025 drivers' title for McLaren, after a close fight with Max Verstappen and his team-mate Oscar Piastri.
explanation.incorrect: The 2025 champion was Lando Norris of McLaren, who edged Max Verstappen in a tight finish.
explanation.sayThisLine: Norris was the 2025 champion, for McLaren.

payload.prompt: Match each champion to a headline moment.

pairs.definition: Won his first title in Abu Dhabi in 2021.
Seven-time champion who moved to Ferrari in 2025.

distractorDefinitions: The first champion, in 1950, with Alfa Romeo.
Won five titles in a row with Ferrari from 2000.

explanation.summary: Three eras in one line: a first title in 2021, the record-equalling Hamilton years, and the newest champion, Norris.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hamilton moved to Ferrari after seven titles.

lessons.title: Senna and Prost
lessons.objective: Explain why the rivalry is F1's defining story.

payload.prompt: Senna and Prost were McLaren teammates in 1988 and 1989. Why is that famous?

options.text: Two all-time greats in the same car fought for the same titles, with no excuses.
options.explanation: Right. Same car, same team, and a rivalry that got personal.

options.text: Senna drove for Ferrari while Prost drove for Williams.
options.explanation: Wrong teams. They were teammates at McLaren, and only later rivals at different teams.

options.text: They were friends on track who never fought.
options.explanation: The opposite. Their battles were intense and sometimes bitter.

options.text: They never raced each other, so the rivalry is a myth.
options.explanation: They raced each other dozens of times, including as teammates.

explanation.correct: Senna and Prost were the two best drivers of their time, in the same car, and neither would give way. That is the purest teammate rivalry in F1 history.
explanation.incorrect: Senna and Prost shared a McLaren in 1988 and 1989 and fought for the titles. It is the classic teammate rivalry.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same car, two greats, no excuses.

payload.prompt: At Suzuka in 1990, Senna clinched the title at the first corner. How?

options.text: He drove into Prost's Ferrari, and later admitted it was deliberate.
options.explanation: Right. Senna said afterwards that he had made up his mind to do it.

options.text: Prost retired on the first lap with a broken engine.
options.explanation: Prost did not retire with a fault. The two collided.

options.text: A safety car bunched the field and Senna passed Prost on the last lap.
options.explanation: That sounds like Abu Dhabi 2021, a different story altogether.

options.text: The stewards gave Prost a penalty for an illegal start.
options.explanation: The collision, not a penalty, settled the title.

explanation.correct: In 1990, Senna, then leading the title, drove into Prost's Ferrari at turn one, ending both their races and sealing the championship. He admitted it later. A year earlier they had collided at Suzuka as teammates, and Prost took the title.
explanation.incorrect: At Suzuka in 1990 Senna drove into Prost's Ferrari at the first corner and won the title. He later admitted it was deliberate.
explanation.sayThisLine: Senna took Prost out at the first corner and won the title.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: Senna and Prost hated each other their whole lives.

payload.question: How do you respond?

options.text: They fought bitterly, but they made peace before Senna died in 1994, and Prost carried his coffin.
options.explanation: Right. The story is a fight that ended in respect.

options.text: Yes, they never spoke to each other again after 1990.
options.explanation: They did patch things up. By 1993 they were on better terms.

options.text: No, they were always best friends and the rivalry was just for the cameras.
options.explanation: The rivalry was real, and it included deliberate collisions.

options.text: Prost was a nobody, so there was nothing to hate.
options.explanation: Prost was a four-time champion, so the rivalry was between two greats.

payload.translation: Senna and Prost had a famously bitter fight in the late 1980s and early 1990s, but they reconciled before Senna's death, and Prost was a pallbearer at his funeral.

followUps.why: Around 1993, after Prost retired. The rivalry mellowed into mutual respect.

followUps.line: Whose side do most fans take?
followUps.why: Fans are split, which is part of why the rivalry is so loved.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you only know the headline, say so and ask which moment they think defined it.

statement.speaker: A fan
statement.text: I only know Senna. Why does Prost matter?

payload.question: What is a fair answer?

options.text: Prost won four titles and was nicknamed the Professor. Senna had to beat him to become a legend.
options.explanation: Right. Prost was one of the best, which is why the rivalry matters.

options.text: He does not matter. He was just the driver Senna beat.
options.explanation: Prost won four titles and often beat Senna.

options.text: Prost won three titles, the same as Senna.
options.explanation: Senna won three. Prost won four.

options.text: Prost was Senna's engineer.
options.explanation: Prost was a driver and Senna's teammate.

payload.translation: Alain Prost won four world titles and was known for a calm, calculated style. Ayrton Senna was raw speed. Together they defined the late 1980s.

followUps.why: He was famous for thinking a race through and keeping the car smooth.
Senna was often the faster over one lap, Prost the better tactician.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can be honest that you know one more than the other. It makes a good question.

payload.prompt: Did Senna and Prost make peace before Senna died in 1994?

scene.alt: Text only: one of F1's most famous rivalries and how it ended.

explanation.correct: They made up around 1993. Senna pulled Prost onto the top step of the podium at the last race of that year, and Prost was a pallbearer at Senna's funeral.
explanation.incorrect: They did patch things up. The fight was real, but it ended in respect, which is part of why fans love the story.
explanation.sayThisLine: They fought like crazy, then respected each other.

lessons.title: Schumacher and the Ferrari years
lessons.objective: Explain why Ferrari's 2000s dominance still shapes fans.

payload.prompt: Where did Michael Schumacher win five of his seven titles?

options.text: Benetton, where he won his first two titles.
options.explanation: He won two at Benetton, in 1994 and 1995. The bigger run came later.

options.text: Ferrari, from 2000 to 2004.
options.explanation: Right. He joined Ferrari in 1996 and won five straight titles from 2000.

options.text: Mercedes, late in his career.
options.explanation: He raced for Mercedes from 2010 to 2012 but did not win a title there.

options.text: Williams, where he started.
options.explanation: Schumacher never drove for Williams. He started at Jordan, then moved to Benetton.

explanation.correct: Schumacher joined Ferrari in 1996 and won five consecutive titles from 2000 to 2004, after winning two with Benetton.
explanation.incorrect: Schumacher won two titles with Benetton and five with Ferrari, all five between 2000 and 2004.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five straight titles with Ferrari, 2000 to 2004.

payload.prompt: Why do the tifosi love the Schumacher era so much?

options.text: He ended a long wait: Ferrari had not won the drivers' title since 1979.
options.explanation: Right. The title drought lasted 21 years, until 2000.

options.text: He was Italian, so he was one of their own.
options.explanation: Schumacher was German. They loved him for winning.

options.text: He won with a car bought from another team.
options.explanation: Ferrari builds its own cars and engines.

options.text: Ferrari fans only care about Italian drivers.
options.explanation: Tifosi loyalty is to the team, not a driver's passport.

explanation.correct: Ferrari's last drivers' title before Schumacher came in 1979. He ended a 21-year wait in 2000 and won five in a row, which is why the tifosi still remember him fondly.
explanation.incorrect: Ferrari had gone from 1979 to 2000 without a drivers' title. Schumacher ended that, then kept winning.
explanation.sayThisLine: He ended a 21-year wait for Ferrari.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: Ferrari is a works team. What does that mean?

payload.question: What is the best answer?

options.text: They build their own car and their own power unit, rather than buying an engine from someone else.
options.explanation: Right. A works team makes both the chassis and the power unit.

options.text: It means Ferrari buys its engine from Mercedes.
options.explanation: That is a customer team. Ferrari builds its own.

options.text: It just means Ferrari has the biggest budget.
options.explanation: Budget is separate. Works status is about building the car and the engine yourself.

options.text: It means the team is owned by a car company.
options.explanation: Ownership is different. A works team builds its own power unit, whoever owns it.

payload.translation: A works team builds its own car and its own power unit. A customer team buys the power unit from a supplier, as some of Ferrari's customers do.

followUps.line: Does a works team always win?
followUps.why: No. Having control helps, but it depends on how well they do the job.
Ferrari supplies customer teams, including Haas and Cadillac.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If someone says works team, ask whether they mean the chassis, the engine or both.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: Schumacher only won because he had a great car.

payload.question: What is the fuller story?

options.text: The car was fast, but he also helped rebuild Ferrari's culture and the team built around him.
options.explanation: Right. Driver and team improved each other.

options.text: The car had nothing to do with it.
options.explanation: A great car is essential in F1. The point is that the driver helped create it.

options.text: Every driver would have won in that car.
options.explanation: Teammates in the same car usually finished behind him.

options.text: Ferrari won only because of rule changes.
options.explanation: Ferrari's rise came from hiring, testing and strategy as well as the car.

payload.translation: Schumacher drove a very fast car, but he also pushed Ferrari to hire well, test harder and work as one team. The dynasty came from both.

followUps.why: Ferrari's engineers and its strategists, working closely with him.

followUps.line: Does that settle the car versus driver debate?
followUps.why: No. It shows why the debate never ends.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A balanced take is a good one here: great driver, great car, great team.

payload.prompt: Complete the Ferrari fan fact.
payload.template: Ferrari's devoted fans are called the {{fans}}, and they waited {{years}} years for a drivers' title before 2000.

explanation.correct: The tifosi are Ferrari's famously loyal fans, and their long wait from 1979 to 2000 is why Schumacher's first title with the team meant so much.
explanation.incorrect: Ferrari fans are the tifosi. Ferrari had not won a drivers' title since 1979, so the wait was 21 years.
explanation.sayThisLine: The tifosi waited twenty-one years for that title.

lessons.title: Hamilton versus Verstappen
lessons.objective: Explain the 2021 finale and why people still argue.

payload.prompt: What happened in the 2021 Abu Dhabi finale between Hamilton and Verstappen?

options.text: Hamilton crashed on the last lap, handing Verstappen the title.
options.explanation: There was no Hamilton crash. The decider was a late restart.

options.text: They were level on points, a late safety car set up a one-lap restart, and Verstappen passed Hamilton for the title.
options.explanation: Right. It was the most dramatic finale in years.

options.text: Hamilton won his eighth title by a big margin.
options.explanation: Hamilton was denied the eighth title, which would have been a record.

options.text: Both drivers collided and neither won the title.
options.explanation: They did not collide. Verstappen passed Hamilton cleanly.

explanation.correct: Hamilton and Verstappen went into the last race level on points. A late safety car set up a one-lap restart, and Verstappen, on fresher tyres, passed Hamilton to win his first title.
explanation.incorrect: Abu Dhabi 2021 was settled on the final lap: a late safety car, a one-lap restart, and Verstappen, on fresher tyres, passing Hamilton.
explanation.sayThisLine: A late safety car, one lap to go, and Verstappen took the title.

payload.prompt: Why is the 2021 safety car decision still argued about?

options.text: Only some lapped cars were allowed to unlap, and the safety car came in a lap early.
options.explanation: Right. That handled the restart in a way fans still disagree about.

options.text: The safety car was not needed because no car had crashed.
options.explanation: A crash had happened, so a safety car was justified. The debate was about the restart.

options.text: The safety car stayed out for the rest of the race.
options.explanation: It came in for a one-lap restart.

options.text: Both drivers were told to pit under the safety car.
options.explanation: That is not what happened, and it is not the argument.

explanation.correct: After a crash, only the lapped cars between the leaders were told to unlap, and the safety car came in a lap early, leaving a one-lap shootout. Many fans thought the rules were applied unusually, which is why it is still argued.
explanation.incorrect: The argument is about the restart: only some lapped cars were allowed to unlap, and the safety car came in at the start of the last lap.
explanation.sayThisLine: The debate is about how the restart was handled.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: Does the 2021 loss diminish Lewis Hamilton's legacy?

payload.question: What is a balanced answer?

options.text: It was painful and controversial, but it does not erase seven titles. He is still one of the greats.
options.explanation: Right. One race does not define a career.

options.text: Yes, it proves he is overrated.
options.explanation: One race does not cancel seven titles and a lot of wins.

options.text: He was robbed, so his career is tainted forever.
options.explanation: That goes too far. It was a controversial ending, not the end of his story.

options.text: It had no effect on anyone.
options.explanation: It mattered a lot to both drivers and to fans, which is why people still argue.

payload.translation: Hamilton lost the 2021 title in a controversial finish, but he already had seven titles. Many fans feel the ending is a footnote to a great career.

followUps.why: He kept racing at Mercedes, then moved to Ferrari in 2025.

followUps.line: Would it have been a record?
followUps.why: Yes. An eighth title would have made him the outright record holder.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can say it was controversial without choosing a side.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: Was the race director's call in 2021 right?

payload.question: What is a fair answer?

options.text: Fans disagree: some say it fit the rules, others say it went against how safety cars normally work.
options.explanation: Right. You described the disagreement without taking a side.

options.text: It was completely fair and nobody should question it.
options.explanation: Many fans and teams did question it, and the rules were later reviewed.

options.text: The officials are obviously corrupt.
options.explanation: That is a claim without evidence. You can disagree with a decision without attacking someone's honesty.

options.text: There was no decision to argue about.
options.explanation: The restart was a real decision, and it is still debated.

payload.translation: The 2021 finale hinged on how the race director handled the safety car restart. Some say it followed the rules, others that it departed from normal practice. The FIA later reviewed its procedures.

followUps.why: Yes. The FIA reviewed the process and changed how race control works.

followUps.line: Which part do you think mattered most?
followUps.why: A good question: the unlapping, or the timing of the restart.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Saying both sides have a point is honest and keeps the conversation friendly.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: How does Hamilton versus Verstappen compare to Senna versus Prost?

payload.question: What is a thoughtful answer?

options.text: Senna and Prost shared a car; Hamilton and Verstappen fought in different cars. Both defined their eras.
options.explanation: Right. The set-up is different, but the intensity was similar.

options.text: They are exactly the same rivalry.
options.explanation: They are not. One was between teammates, the other between two top teams.

options.text: Hamilton and Verstappen were teammates too.
options.explanation: They raced for Mercedes and Red Bull, rival teams.

options.text: Nobody remembers the older one.
options.explanation: Senna and Prost are still one of F1's most discussed rivalries.

payload.translation: Senna and Prost were teammates in one team. Hamilton and Verstappen were rivals in different cars. Both fights pushed the sport into the spotlight.

followUps.why: Fans argue about it. Both had controversial collisions.

followUps.line: Do you rate one more than the other?
followUps.why: A friendly question that keeps a good chat going.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: There is no correct ranking here, so just enjoy the comparison.

lessons.title: Iconic circuits
lessons.objective: Match legendary circuits to what makes them special.

payload.prompt: Why is Monaco so revered?

options.text: It is a tight street circuit with walls everywhere, so pole position is almost worth the race.
options.explanation: Right. Overtaking is hard and mistakes are punished.

options.text: It has the longest straight on the calendar, so overtaking is easy.
options.explanation: Monaco has short straights and is famous for being hard to pass on.

options.text: It is famous only because rich people attend.
options.explanation: The glamour is real, but the prestige comes from the challenge and the history.

options.text: It is the only street circuit in F1.
options.explanation: It is not. Several other races are held on city streets.

explanation.correct: Monaco is narrow, bumpy and lined with walls. Overtaking is very difficult, so qualifying matters more here than at almost any other track.
explanation.incorrect: Monaco is tight and walled, so track position is almost everything. That is why pole is so valuable.
explanation.sayThisLine: At Monaco, qualifying is almost the race.

payload.prompt: Silverstone in the UK is famous for which type of corner?

options.text: Slow hairpins where overtaking happens.
options.explanation: Silverstone has fast corners, not slow hairpins.

options.text: High-speed corners like Copse and Maggotts-Becketts, where downforce is the story.
options.explanation: Right. Silverstone is famous for corners taken at high speed, where the car's downforce and the driver's skill combine.

options.text: Tight street-circuit corners like Monaco.
options.explanation: Silverstone is a traditional circuit, not a street circuit. It has long straights and high-speed corners.

options.text: Technical low-grip corners where tyre management matters most.
options.explanation: Grip is high at Silverstone. Downforce and speed are the keys.

explanation.correct: Right. Silverstone is fast. Maggotts and Becketts are taken at high speed, flat-out or nearly so. Downforce and bravery are the story.
explanation.incorrect: Silverstone is known for its high-speed corners, especially the Maggotts-Becketts sequence. Drivers attack these corners at speed, and the fastest car dominates.
explanation.sayThisLine: Silverstone is where fast corners and brave drivers define the winner.

payload.prompt: Match each circuit to what it is famous for.

pairs.definition: A tight street circuit where qualifying is almost the race.
A night race on city streets, hot, humid and physically hard.
The Temple of Speed: very fast, low drag and Ferrari's home race.

distractorDefinitions: A desert circuit famous for its mountain passes.
A short oval used for qualifying.

explanation.summary: Monaco is about precision, Singapore is a night street race that wears drivers out, and Monza is about top speed and the tifosi.
explanation.sayThisLine: Monza is the Temple of Speed.

payload.prompt: Match the Triple Crown facts.

pairs.definition: Win the Monaco Grand Prix, the Indianapolis 500 and the 24 Hours of Le Mans.
The only driver to win all three, completing it in 1972.
Three different kinds of racing, in different series and countries.

explanation.summary: The Triple Crown spans F1, American oval racing and endurance racing. Graham Hill is the only driver to have completed it.
explanation.sayThisLine: Graham Hill is the only Triple Crown winner.

payload.prompt: Match each circuit type to its character.

pairs.definition: Long straights, low drag wings and the slipstream matters.
Walls close, little run-off, and track position is key.
Downforce and bravery decide lap time.

distractorDefinitions: Pit-lane only races where tyres do not matter.

explanation.summary: Each track type rewards something different, which is why teams change their set-up from race to race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Different tracks, different cars.

lessons.title: How F1 got safer
lessons.objective: Explain milestones like the halo and modern crash structures.

payload.prompt: The halo is a safety device introduced in 2018. What does it protect?

options.text: The driver's head and upper body from debris and impacts.
options.explanation: Right. The halo is a titanium bar above the cockpit that keeps dangerous objects away from the driver's head.

options.text: The entire cockpit; it is a full cage around the car.
options.explanation: No. The halo is just a bar. The monocoque is the full survival cell.

options.text: The tyres and suspension from hitting other cars.
options.explanation: No. The halo protects the driver's head.

options.text: The fuel tank from leaking.
options.explanation: That is not the halo's job. Modern safety includes the halo, but also fuel-cell design.

explanation.correct: Right. The halo is a titanium bar above the cockpit. It has saved drivers from head injuries many times since 2018.
explanation.incorrect: The halo is a curved titanium bar positioned above the driver's cockpit. It deflects debris, wheels, and parts away from the head. It has been credited with saving multiple drivers' lives.
explanation.sayThisLine: The halo has saved driver's lives multiple times since 2018.

payload.prompt: Complete the safety basics.
payload.template: The {{cell}} is the carbon-fibre survival cell around the driver, and the {{bar}} is a titanium bar that shields his {{part}}.

explanation.correct: The monocoque is the rigid survival cell the driver sits in. The halo sits above it and deflects debris and other cars away from the head.
explanation.incorrect: The monocoque is the survival cell, and the halo is a titanium bar above it that protects the driver's head.
explanation.sayThisLine: The monocoque is the survival cell, and the halo guards the head.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: After the tragedies of 1994, has F1 really got safer?

payload.question: What is the honest answer?

options.text: Yes, a lot: stronger cars, better barriers, better medical response, and later the halo. Motorsport is still risky.
options.explanation: Right. The sport changed a great deal, and it still takes the risk seriously.

options.text: No, it is exactly as dangerous as before.
options.explanation: Safety has improved hugely since the 1990s.

options.text: Yes, it is now completely safe.
options.explanation: It is much safer, but it is never completely safe.

options.text: Only the cars changed, not the circuits.
options.explanation: Circuits, barriers and medical teams all changed too.

payload.translation: After the deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, F1 changed car design, barriers, circuits and medical response. The halo came in 2018.

followUps.why: Cockpit sides got higher, crash tests got stricter and medical cars and doctors became standard.

followUps.line: Was there one big turning point?
followUps.why: 1994 is often named as the start of the modern safety era.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: This is a sombre topic. Keep it respectful and do not joke about it.

statement.speaker: A friend
statement.text: In 2020, Romain Grosjean's car split in two in a fireball, and he walked away. How?

payload.question: What is the best answer?

options.text: The halo and the survival cell protected him, and the medical and fire crews reacted fast.
options.explanation: Right. It was the result of years of safety work.

options.text: He was just lucky, and safety had nothing to do with it.
options.explanation: Luck played a part, but the halo, the cell and the rescue team were critical.

options.text: The crash was not as bad as it looked.
options.explanation: It was a severe crash and a very serious fire.

options.text: The car was fully made of steel.
options.explanation: Modern F1 cars are made mostly of carbon fibre.

payload.translation: At Bahrain in 2020 Grosjean's car hit a barrier and caught fire. The halo helped keep the barrier away from his head, the survival cell held, and the rescue team got him out.

followUps.why: It was red-flagged while the barrier was repaired, then restarted.
At first, some disliked how it looked. Incidents since then have mostly ended that argument.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Serious crashes deserve a respectful tone. Keep the conversation about the safety work.

payload.prompt: Why is a race red-flagged after a serious crash?

options.text: To stop the race so marshals and medics can work safely and the track or barriers can be repaired.
options.explanation: Right. A safety car is not enough for a big repair.

options.text: To end the race and give points on the current order.
options.explanation: A red flag pauses the race. It usually restarts unless it cannot be resumed.

options.text: To punish the driver who crashed.
options.explanation: Red flags are about safety, not punishment.

options.text: To let the television broadcast ads.
options.explanation: The reason is safety and repair, not television.

explanation.correct: A red flag stops the race so crews can work safely. Teams can change tyres, and the race restarts once it is safe, which is why it feels like a new race.
explanation.incorrect: A red flag is for when the track needs proper repair or rescue work. It pauses the race rather than ending it.
explanation.sayThisLine: A red flag pauses the race while everyone works safely.

lessons.title: How to watch a race together
lessons.objective: Plan a watch-party and follow the race without over-asking.

payload.prompt: When is the best time to ask your friend a question during the race?

options.text: During a lull, like a safety car or the pit-stop window.
options.explanation: Right. That is when they can explain without missing action.

options.text: At the start, while the cars are on the first lap.
options.explanation: The start is the most intense moment. Save the question.

options.text: On the final lap, just before the chequered flag.
options.explanation: Do not interrupt the finish. Ask afterwards.

options.text: Every lap, so you do not forget.
options.explanation: Constant questions get tiring. A few good ones are better.

explanation.correct: Safety cars, pit stops and red flags are natural pauses. Your friend can chat, and you get the answer while the situation is fresh.
explanation.incorrect: Wait for a lull. Ask during a safety car or pit stop, and stay quiet for starts and finishes.
explanation.sayThisLine: What just happened? I'll wait for the safety car to ask.

payload.prompt: A safety car comes out while your friend's driver leads. Pit or stay out?

situation.narrative: Your friend's driver leads by 10 seconds, but the safety car bunches the field and erases the gap. His tyres are old and there are 20 laps to go.

options.label: Pit for fresh tyres.
options.consequence: The stop costs about half as much as usual, and he restarts on fresh tyres with 20 laps to go.
considerations: The safety car has already erased his gap.
Old tyres could fade badly over 20 laps.

options.label: Stay out and keep the lead.
options.consequence: He keeps the lead but restarts on worn tyres. Rivals on fresh tyres can attack him for 20 laps.
considerations: Track position matters, but worn tyres cost pace.
Rivals who pit get a free stop.

options.label: Wait a lap to see what the others do.
options.consequence: He may still get a cheap stop, but he risks the safety car ending before he commits.
considerations: The cheap-stop window closes when the field is released.

payload.expertNote: A safety car makes a stop cheap, so strategists often pit on the spot. The team pays with track position only if the others do not pit.
payload.sayThisLine: The safety car made the stop cheap, so he took fresh tyres.

payload.prompt: Your friend is anxious before a last-lap restart. What do you do?

situation.narrative: The field has been bunched by a safety car. One lap to go. Your friend's driver is second, close behind the leader.

facts.label: Race
facts.value: Final lap after a safety car

facts.label: Your friend's driver
facts.value: Second, within a second of the leader

options.label: Stay quiet, maybe give them a squeeze of the arm.
options.consequence: They feel supported and can focus. You can talk about it after.
considerations: The last lap is the most tense moment.
Silence can be the kindest thing.

options.label: Ask them to explain the restart rules.
options.consequence: It breaks their focus at the worst moment. Save the question for later.
considerations: This is not a teaching moment.

options.label: Cheer loudly for their driver.
options.consequence: A little enthusiasm can be fun, but follow their lead. If they are quiet, match it.
considerations: Let your friend set the tone.

payload.expertNote: The last lap belongs to the person who cares most. Match their mood and save the questions for the chequered flag.
payload.sayThisLine: I'm right here. Let's watch this.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He is three seconds behind. He can catch him before the end.

payload.question: What is a fair reply?

options.text: It depends how many laps are left. Closing three seconds needs a few tenths a lap, so it is tough with only a few laps to go.
options.explanation: Right. You used the gap and the laps remaining, and you stayed kind.

options.text: Three seconds is nothing. He will catch him easily.
options.explanation: It is a real gap. Without many laps or a mistake, it is hard to close.

options.text: Three seconds is exactly one pit stop, so he has to pit.
options.explanation: A pit stop costs about twenty seconds, not three.

options.text: Nobody ever catches anyone once the gap is over a second.
options.explanation: Cars do close gaps, especially on fresher tyres or with a mistake ahead.

payload.translation: A three-second gap can be closed if the chaser is a few tenths quicker per lap and there are enough laps. With only a few left, it is hard.

followUps.why: That is the key number to know when judging a chase.
Fresh tyres are usually what lets a driver close a gap.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can be hopeful and realistic at once. Asking the laps left is a real-fan question.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: He finished second. I wanted the win, but he drove well.

payload.question: How do you respond?

options.text: Second on a day like that is a great result, and he earned it. What was your favourite moment?
options.explanation: Right. You celebrated the result and invited them to share the race.

options.text: Sorry he lost. That must feel awful.
options.explanation: That amplifies the disappointment. They already said he drove well.

options.text: Second is the first loser, so it does not count.
options.explanation: A podium is a big result, and it is not kind to dismiss it.

options.text: The winner only won because of luck.
options.explanation: That is unfair to the winner, and it does not help your friend feel better.

payload.translation: After a good second place, celebrate what went well and invite your friend to talk about the race.

followUps.why: Asking for their favourite moment lets them relive the race.
Looking at the gap helps them see how well he did.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to analyse the race. Asking what they enjoyed is enough.

payload.title: Watch party surprise
payload.setting: After the race, your friend wants to talk about a pit-stop call they didn't understand.

exchanges.theirMessage: Why did the pit wall pit so early? We were leading, and the tyres were fine.

replies.text: Was there a car closing in? Sometimes you pit early to cover a threat.
replies.coachNote: You asked a clarifying question to help them think through the strategy.
replies.theirResponse: Oh, I didn't notice the gap closing. That makes sense.

replies.text: Let me ask: how close was the second-place car? Sometimes the pit wall sees a threat and stops early to cover it.
replies.coachNote: You invited them to analyze the situation and explained the pit wall's perspective.
replies.theirResponse: Wow, I was too focused on the leader to notice. That is smart strategy.

replies.text: They made a mistake. Early stops usually lose the race.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing the pit wall's call without understanding it misses the learning moment.

payload.closingNote: A pit call that looks early might be a strategic response to a threat. The pit wall sees the gaps; ask about their reasoning instead of judging the call.
